prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 regime

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. As Chair I have taken the point in my own summary that the committee's opening rankings partly drove the move toward B042, so I tested it again on its own evidence rather than on the support count. The core is a distinct idea. A lattice at the magic wavelength makes the light shift equal for the two clock states, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is different in kind from the comb (2005), which counts optical cycles, and from the single-ion control (2012), which uses one trapped quantum system. It was demonstrated in the laboratory, rebuilt independently at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and elsewhere, and the clocks agree when compared at about 1e-18. As an instrument builder, that is the test I trust most: a new measurement capability that others can reproduce and that opens experiments nobody could do before. The millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measured inside a single sample is already a laboratory result. Attribution is compact and can be written into the citation: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and first strontium demonstrations, Ye for taking the clock to the accuracy and stability frontier and for the many-body physics of the lattice. I would keep it to two names and one part.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still novelty against 2005 and 2012, and Danielsson's conditional support shows that it is not trivial. If a reviewer reads the citation as 'better clocks', the prize looks like a third award in precision metrology. The second is attribution: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made real contributions to the 1e-18 performance, and the Al+ ion clocks are a parallel route. A two-name credit leaves them out and the reasons should be on the record. Third, the fundamental-physics payoff is mostly prospective. To my knowledge the strongest bounds on varying constants have come as much from ion clocks as from lattice clocks, and dark-matter searches with lattice clocks have so far produced limits, not signals. I cannot verify the current numbers here and would ask the expert reports to state which bounds are actually competitive. Fourth, the pending redefinition of the second is a metrological milestone outside the physics itself, and I do not want it to decide the timing. Finally, B042 is outside my own expertise, so I rely on Lindroth, Johansson and Kroll for priority questions.

responses.point: Lattice clocks are an invention and a precision frontier rather than a discovery about nature, no deviation from general relativity or the Standard Model has been seen, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes make this a smaller step; you support B042 conditionally on evidence of competitive physics bounds.
responses.response: I think your condition is fair, and I would answer it in two parts. Honestly, the bounds on constants and dark-matter couplings so far are null results, and I am not sure the lattice clocks lead those searches over the best ion clocks. I do not want to overstate that in a citation, which is why mine does not claim new tests of fundamental physics. What the lattice clock has delivered as physics is a measurement that was not possible before: a gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre in one atomic sample, and clock comparisons that agree at 1e-18. The Nobel record also includes prizes for new measurement capability, such as gravitational-wave detection, where the first physics results were also confirmations. If the expert reports show that no competitive bound exists and that the committee wants a discovery about nature first, I would hold B029 as my fallback instead of adding any other name. I do not think the absence of a deviation from the Standard Model disqualifies an instrument that opens the regime.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model) followed by decisive experiment, tuned by a purely geometric parameter, and speed of reproduction by independent groups should count; you asked whether a maturity argument undervalues that speed.
responses.response: I accept that the speed and breadth of reproduction is an important point, and my round-1 answer was too short on it. Many groups have confirmed the correlated insulators and superconducting domes, and the continuum model predicted the flat bands quantitatively. That is strong science and I would not call it a weak candidate. Where I still differ is in what has been confirmed. Reproduction shows the phases exist; it does not yet tell us what they are. You, Lindroth and Johansson all describe the pairing mechanism as unsettled, and twist-angle disorder limits how intrinsic the phases are. A citation would have to be worded around the phenomenon without saying what it is, and the attribution gap to Cao, Fatemi and earlier theory is also open. The clocks have both reproduction and a settled interpretation. So I do not think I am undervaluing speed. I am weighing settled interpretation more heavily, and I would expect B054 to be a stronger case after a few more years, so please keep it as a live candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Topological insulators are a new class of quantum matter with a stable Z2 classification confirmed in many materials, distinct from the 2016 prize, so a new kind of matter should weigh more than another precision gain; the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu is the weak point of your own choice.
responses.response: I agree that a new kind of matter is a larger conceptual step than another digit of precision, and your own acknowledgement of the credit problem is what keeps me from supporting B007. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leaves out the people who proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp tested, as well as Fu, Moore and Hasan in three dimensions. Expert reports would likely treat this as a contested decision. I cannot assess the overlap with 2016 myself and you have not yet put a number on it. On your general point I disagree in one respect: a new measurement regime that many experiments can use, such as the lattice clock, has a weight of its own and need not rank below a new phase. If you can show a three-name credit that does not exclude these theorists, I would reopen B007. Until then I would treat your fallback to B042 as the best reading of the committee.

responses.point: The citation should rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and its demonstration, with Katori credited for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for the accuracy and stability frontier, and you would not add a third name; the primary-literature evidence for any third contributor is still unsettled.
responses.response: Your reading is the one I am relying on, and my citation follows it: the idea of the magic-wavelength trap and its realisation, not clocks or combs in general. On the third-name question from my own summary, I looked for a case that would displace either name. Lemonde and Derevianko did contribute early theory and the SYRTE and PTB groups made decisive contributions to the accuracy budgets, but I have no primary-literature evidence that would let me argue that any of them is more decisive than Ye. I would not add a name. I do want the committee's record to state why they are excluded, as Johansson asked. I would also welcome your check of whether the early lattice-clock theory predates Katori's proposal in a way that changes the order of credit.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports find that lattice-clock comparisons have yielded competitive bounds on varying constants, dark matter or gravity, and not only prospective ones.
Whether the citation wording separates the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice clearly enough from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether early lattice-clock theory (Derevianko, Lemonde) or the Al+ ion-clock tradition carries a claim that would change the credited names.

Whether the committee will accept a set of null results and a metrology milestone as a discovery-level achievement, since I cannot rule out that a different weight on discovery would favour B029 or B054 in a later year.
Whether B054 and B007 might become stronger candidates in a later year once the pairing mechanism and the attribution questions are clearer.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no collaboration with Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups, and B042 is outside my expertise. I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and have professional familiarity with the neutrino-astronomy community around B029 and the gamma-ray and black-hole community around B047; I am not in IceCube or the EHT. Since my own round-1 summary shows B042 is the leading position and I now propose it, B029 and B047 are not the leading proposals, so I do not see a recusal question. I would raise it at once if either of them became the leading proposal. The other members' disclosures (Kroll, Olsson, Lindroth, Johansson) do not seem to me to require any special handling for a B042 vote, as they are collegial or institutional and not collaborations with Katori or Ye.
